entries.title: Blackhawks' Kevin Korchinski hopes to 'prove I belong' in back-against-wall season
entries.summary: <p>The last three years have been a rocky road for defenseman <b>Kevin Korchinski</b>,<b> Kyle Davidson’s</b> first draft pick as the Blackhawks’ general manager in 2022.</p><p>It hasn’t been all bad, but things haven’t gone exactly the way Korchinski or the Hawks would have hoped since he turned pro.</p><p>Korchinski, 22, now enters his fourth pro season in a make-or-break situation. He’s no longer exempt from waivers, which basically locks him into an NHL roster spot — at least for now — because the Hawks won’t risk losing a top-10 selection that easily.</p><p>But playing time is far from guaranteed. Davidson has said he’s more comfortable than ever with young players sitting out as healthy scratches now that the Hawks are prioritizing trying to win every night.</p><p>Coach <b>Jeff Blashill</b> has said Korchinski appears more confident and his skating ‘‘more controlled.’’ But he also admitted Sunday that Korchinski isn’t one of the Hawks’ top six defensemen right now.</p><p>Korchinski looked like arguably the best player on the ice in the Hawks’ first preseason matchup with the Wild on Saturday, when the teams predominantly dressed AHL rosters. But he wasn’t part of the largely NHL lineup that earned a 4-3 overtime victory in the rematch Monday.</p><p>Korchinski will have to earn every regular-season game and minute, and he understands that.</p><p>‘‘[My goal is to] prove I belong here and that I want to be part of this culture,’’ he said.</p><p>Korchinksi has been limited in the past by his subpar strength against NHL competition. He couldn’t, for example, consistently box out opponents around his net. That’s part of why the Hawks have been outscored 95-52 in his 105 NHL games to date.</p><p>He hopes he has addressed that weakness. He’s now 198 pounds, up 10 from the end of last season but roughly the same as he was last September. But not all changes are reflected in weight.</p><p>‘‘I definitely got stronger and my gym numbers got better,’’ Korchinski said. ‘‘My approach, rather than gaining a lot of weight, [was] more trying to get stronger.’’</p><h3>Preseason victory</h3><p>A victory was expected Monday, considering the Hawks dressed a far superior lineup than the Wild. <b>Bowen Byram </b>eventually gave them that by completing a hat trick in his unofficial first appearance at the United Center with the Hawks.</p><p><b>Patrick Kane</b> didn’t play, but Byram, <b>Nick Lardis</b> and <b>Roman Kantserov </b>were standouts.</p><p>Blashill liked how the Hawks held on to pucks longer in the offensive zone, but he noted they gave up too many odd-man rushes and showed signs of fatigue after five consecutive grueling days of training camp.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bowen Byram OT WINNER FOR THE HAT TRICK! <a href="https://t.co/ez9IihRNAC">pic.twitter.com/ez9IihRNAC</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2102223892496757214?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Commesso belongs</b></h3><p>Goalie prospect <b>Drew Commesso</b> also gained some weight during the summer, adding six pounds to get up to 190.</p><p>‘‘The biggest area I feel it in is my legs,’’ Commesso said. ‘‘My leg strength around the posts, I did a ton of work on that this summer. Comparing video from last year, I definitely see a difference. The NHL is really fast, so if I can improve just a millisecond, it’s going to lead to more saves.’’</p><p>After earning his first two NHL victories and first shutout last season, the 24-year-old now sees himself as an NHL-caliber goalie.</p><p>‘‘I belong at that level, and [I have] the mindset that I’m there,’’ he said. ‘‘That allows me to carry myself a little differently in a lot of good ways.’’</p><p>Commesso won’t start this season at the NHL level, but opportunities should come his way during the season. With a new two-year contract in hand, he could take over as the Hawks’ full-time backup by next season.</p>

entries.title: Chicago police fatally shoot dog that attacked them in Humboldt Park
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police shot and killed a dog that attacked them while the officers were working on an investigation in the Humboldt Park neighborhood Monday, police said.</p><p>Shortly before 5 p.m., the officers were in the 700 block of North Christiana Avenue when a dog approached and attacked an officer. One of the officers then shot the dog. </p><p>The dog died and the city's Department of Animal Care and Control was notified.</p><p>Three officers were taken to nearby hospitals in good condition. No other injuries were reported.</p><p>Detectives are continuing to investigate the incident.</p>

entries.title: For Blackhawks, Jordan Greenway's defensive acumen makes him sneaky-smart addition
entries.summary: <p>While the hockey world erupted into furious debate over the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ blockbuster trade for defenseman Bowen Byram in June, one piece flew under the radar.</p><p>Veteran forward Jordan Greenway quietly came to Chicago in the deal. Although his inclusion might have been a salary dump on the Sabres’ end — his $4 million salary-cap hit was outsized for his role in their lineup — it was welcomed on the Hawks’ end.</p><p>‘‘Jordan brings a heaviness, a physicality to our group that we could use,’’ general manager Kyle Davidson said afterward. ‘‘He’s a really big body that can get in on the forecheck and make life difficult for opposing -defenders.’’</p><p>The Hawks enter this season with two scrappy forwards — Greenway and Andrew Mangiapane — whom contenders were eager to dump last spring but whom they consider to be worthwhile buy-low experiments.</p><p>It appears both will have spots in the opening-night lineup. Mangiapane has skated on the third line with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/20/blackhawks-oliver-moore-nick-lardis-depth-roles-training" target="_blank" >Oliver Moore</a> and Ryan Donato so far.</p><p>Greenway has skated on the fourth — alongside Ryan Greene and free-agent signing Cole Smith — while playing on the penalty kill, as well.</p><p>The Hawks are optimistic about the potential impact on the fourth line, aside from the nickname confusion with two guys called ‘‘Greener’’ skating side-by-side.</p><p>‘‘It’s a line I would feel very comfortable putting out against anybody,’’ coach Jeff Blashill said.</p><p>You also could say it’s an eco-friendly line. Greenway apparently suggested an alternative nickname — a surely not-work-appropriate one — that Blashill refuses to use.</p><p>It’s possible Greenway will end up being the Pat Maroon of this Hawks team. Like Maroon, he’s massive (6-6 and 231 pounds), sometimes silly off the ice and sometimes mean on it.</p><p>But it’s also possible Greenway, unlike Maroon, will end up becoming a significant depth contributor for these Hawks.</p><p>‘‘I don’t know if it’s unfortunately or fortunately, but I think I’m a little bit older on this team, which is kind of nuts,’’ Greenway said Monday. ‘‘[I’m] just trying to lead these guys, bring some confidence to the squad. On the ice, I’ll continue to do as I do: play a power forward-type game, create some space and bring a physical presence.’’</p><p>There was a time during the first chapter of Greenway’s career with the Wild when he formed one-third of one of the most effective shutdown lines in the NHL.</p><p>In 2021 and 2022, the Wild trio of Greenway, Joel Eriksson Ek and Marcus Foligno regularly faced opponents’ best players and dominated them. In 749 minutes together across two seasons, that line outscored opponents 45-16 with a 57.6% scoring-chance ratio.</p><p>‘‘I’ve been doing it my whole career,’’ Greenway said. ‘‘I enjoy playing against the top lines, trying to shut them down and frustrate them.’’</p><p>He was similarly effective in 2023-24 with the Sabres, too, albeit without such consistent linemates. He chipped in 28 points and racked up 141 hits.</p><p>Analytics models rated him as one of the best defensive forwards in the league that season, which is worth noting, even though Blashill recently made the case NHL analytics haven’t yet figured out how to evaluate defensive play accurately.</p><p>Greenway wasn’t able to maintain that momentum the last two seasons, though. Hernia problems limited him to 74 games, during which his production and ice time declined and his analytics worsened.</p><p>He is healthy now, and he’s still in his 20s until February. He’s excited about this new opportunity in Chicago afforded to him by the trade, even if the debate it stirred up didn’t involve him.</p><p>‘‘It’s a great group here,’’ he said. ‘‘You can see how motivated the guys are. They’re trying to make a name for themselves and really do some good things. If we can all start off strong from the get-go, if we can find [out] what we need to do early, we’ll be good.’’</p>

entries.title: Man suspected of fatally slicing woman's neck in Englewood taken into custody
entries.summary: <p>A man who apparently plunged a knife into the neck of a woman, killing her, has been arrested and was in critical condition at a hospital after the early Tuesday attack in Englewood. </p><p>The woman was found lying on the ground with a stab wound to her neck in the 7300 block of South Emerald Avenue around 1:40 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>The unidentified woman was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Officers who were searching the early discovered the apparent attacker, a man who was found on a nearby porch with a cut to his right hand, police said. </p><p>He was also taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition and was placed under arrest, according to police, who said the knife used to kill the woman was recovered. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating and no charges have been announced.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: I attend friends' events, but many skipped my mother's memorial
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mom died of extreme old age recently. She was a sweet woman everyone loved. I sent invitations to her memorial, and I'm getting a lot of excuses for why my friends can't attend. I am upset.</p><p>In my circle of friends (all similar ages), I was the last to graduate, get a career job, start a relationship, buy a house, be married and so forth. I've attended my friends' graduations, weddings, baby showers, milestone birthdays, and family funerals, yet there hasn't been much reciprocation.</p><p>Excuses for not attending Mom's memorial included going to a grandkid's soccer game and attending a 2-year-old's birthday party. Really? I know I'm dealing with unusually strong emotions due to Mom's death, but I want to scream, "This is MY MOM," not some distant friend or relative. My spouse says I shouldn't stress and that all we need is each other (said by someone who has a huge, loving family whereas my family is just me and my dad). How do I deal with my feelings of resentment, abandonment and being a low priority? — <i>LAST ONE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR LAST ONE:</b> Your spouse is right. In the final analysis, all you need is each other — though a few supportive friends would certainly be welcome. I have always said that funerals are for the living, not the deceased. Be grateful for the support you are receiving from the people who accepted the invitation to your mother's funeral. They are your core support group; the others are mere acquaintances, so start thinking of them in those terms.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I rent a two-bedroom apartment, which I shared with my best friend. When he moved away last month due to a work relocation, I advertised the room, and a couple moved in. They are friendly and pay their rent on time, but their cooking produces extremely strong smells that I cannot tolerate. My medication causes hypersensitivity to odors, and I can no longer stand to be in the kitchen because the smells linger. They also live on a very different schedule from me. As a result, my diet and sleep are both suffering. They remain unaware of how the adjustment has affected me because I don't feel they are doing anything wrong.</p><p>I would like to move out into a studio of my own. The lease on this apartment is currently a month-to-month, so the only thing keeping me here is the guilt I feel about burdening my roommates with this. They will have to move out, find a replacement for me or take on the full rent themselves. I want to do right by them, but I know it would be best for me to leave. What is the proper course of action here? — <i>DOOMED IN AUSTRALIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DOOMED:</b> There is no reason why you should feel guilty for leveling with this couple; your health must come first. Explain the problem to them and tell them that while you like them personally, your health is being affected by the cooking odors. Tell them that because you are now on a month-to-month lease, you plan to move to a smaller place of your own and give them the option of staying or moving. Consider this a first step in learning to stand up for yourself.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gregory Donald Gay, 81, is the longtime pastor of the Prayer Center Church of God in Christ in Woodlawn. Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music,” about his sisters’ influential singing group. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As the younger brother of the Gay Sisters gospel group, he had a front row seat for the action<b> </b>during gospel’s golden age. Now, he is sharing his tales in a recently released book, “Can I Get a Witness! Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music” (The University of Chicago Press). The text was co-written with Steven B. Dolins, 69-year-old founder and president of The Sirens Records music label in Highland Park.</p><p>Gay said his sisters would have been forgotten without Dolins.</p><p>“I'm grateful for him opening up a window and letting the general public look in,” Gay said. “They were great, talented people, but I don't think they got a fair break.”</p><p>Gay’s late siblings — Evelyn, Geraldine and Mildred — performed, recorded or rubbed elbows with Ward, Jackson, Sam Cooke, the Staple Singers, James Cleveland, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins. They released music on the legendary Savoy, Decca and Chess labels; toured the country and helped bring gospel to a televised audience. Their 1951 hit record, “God Will Take Care of You,” was later covered by Aretha Franklin.</p><p>But their accomplishments have been overlooked, and their records are difficult to find beyond streaming sites or YouTube.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fc0000" name="image-fc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/439cef1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/012bc3b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6149c15/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Copies of Steven B. entries.title: School Board candidate defends disciplining his kids, says school staff should never use corporal punishment
entries.summary: <p>Fifteen years ago, in the wake of a contentious divorce, the ex-wife of a candidate currently running to be Chicago’s school board president told a judge she wanted an emergency change of custody after her teenage son came to her with a swollen face and scratches, saying he’d gotten them from his father, Victor Henderson.</p><p>One of Henderson’s opponents has seized on the allegations as evidence that he’s unfit to lead the school board.</p><p>Henderson acknowledges that he disciplined his children, but denies that he ever abused them. He told WBEZ and Chalkbeat in a statement that “the court never suspended my parenting time, it never ordered supervised visits, and it did not restrict my relationship with my children.”</p><p>Immediately after the ex-wife’s allegations, the court ordered the children to stay with their mother. But court records reviewed by WBEZ show that Henderson resumed having overnight, unsupervised parenting time with his children.</p><p>After <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/candidate-for-chicago-school-board-president-faced-abuse-allegations-court-records-show/3980275/" target="_blank" ><u>NBC5 first reported the story</u></a> in late August, Jessica Biggs, another candidate for school board president, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/biggs4chicago/status/2092999558665998473" target="_blank" ><u>wrote on the social media platform X</u></a>: “Someone with a history of domestic violence and corporal punishment should not be in a leadership position, especially not for children.”</p><p>Corporal punishment is legal in Illinois but banned in Illinois schools. To decide if corporal punishment is “excessive,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.isba.org/sections/childlaw/newsletter/2015/04/whendoescorporalpunishmentbecomeexc" target="_blank" ><u>a court would typically consider</u></a> the age of the child, if they were injured and how badly and whether the child experienced any trauma from the discipline.</p><p>In a statement, Henderson drew a distinction between what parents may do to discipline their children and what school staff can do. “Teachers should never use corporal punishment with students,” he said.</p><p>The position of school board president is unpaid, but powerful, as that person controls what makes it on the agenda. Some see this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" ><u>heated fourway race</u></a> as a proxy for the upcoming mayoral election and an opportunity to seize control of the school board from the Chicago Teachers Union. Right now, a majority of board members are aligned with the CTU. As of Friday, $2.1 million had poured into the race.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" self-funding his campaign and has not picked up any endorsements from political groups. But he is supported by U.S. Reps. Danny K. Davis and Robin Kelly and several pastors of big Black churches. He has raised a significant amount of money from individuals, including many lawyers.</p><p>To supporters of Henderson, the only Black candidate, the focus on his ex-wife’s allegations amounts to a “smear campaign” with racist undertones. Hermene Hartman, who is working on Henderson’s campaign, <a class="Link" href="https://ndigo.com/2026/09/02/victor-henderson-the-father-vs-victor-henderson-school-board-president/" target="_blank" ><u>wrote in an opinion piece in N’DIGO</u></a>, the online journal she founded, that the incident “is really about a Black man punishing his son.”</p><p>“We should not turn cultural differences into convenient political weapons,” she wrote. “Bravo, Victor, for raising your sons to be young men with firm discipline.”</p><p>Henderson, in an <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/politics/wgn-the-point-politics-chicago-illinois/exclusive-chicago-school-board-president-candidate-responds-to-abuse-allegations/" target="_blank" ><u>interview with WGN’s Tahman Bradley</u></a>, said the criticism shows a lack of cultural understanding.</p><p>“I had to raise my children,” he said, noting he took them to church, school, soccer and basketball games and chess matches. “On a rare occasion, if my children needed to be disciplined because they weren’t adhering to the household rules or even did something that was pretty bad, then, as a father, as an African American father, as a Black father, I had to address it. The alternative was to let my kids run amok, and that wasn’t going to happen.”</p><h3>Henderson kept custody of kids in messy legal battle, records show</h3><p>Henderson says his current relationship with all of his now-adult children is “fantastic” and that they have been involved in his school board campaign. But officials with Henderson’s campaign said the sons did not want to talk about what had been a “painful period” in the family’s history.</p><p>Henderson’s ex-wife, through her attorney, declined to comment.</p><p>The Cook County Circuit Court only has online records from 2012 onward, making it difficult to piece together everything that happened in Henderson’s divorce and custody case.</p><p>Some details are clear: Henderson filed for divorce in 2004 and it was finalized in 2008. Henderson and his wife split custody of their two sons, with the boys alternating weeks at their homes. By 2011, Henderson had remarried.</p><p>In January 2011, Henderson’s ex-wife filed an emergency change of custody petition.</p><p>In the custody petition, which was included in a separate filing from 2012, she alleged that their older son told her that Henderson once repeatedly beat him with the wooden handle of a garden hoe, and smashed his iPhone and iPad. The son said Henderson dropped him off the next day at a homeless shelter and told him to volunteer. When the boy learned he was too young to volunteer, he went to his mother’s office and recounted what happened.</p><p>The ex-wife said in the petition that her son’s face was “inflamed” and she saw scratches and bruises. There’s no indication that she called the police. But she said she called her son’s therapist that day and that her son recounted the same story to the therapist. She said her son also told her and the therapist that Henderson “will sometimes” come into his bedroom at night in a “violent rage” and “whip him with a belt when he is asleep under the covers.”</p><p>The judge’s initial reaction was to handwrite an order keeping the boys temporarily with the mom until a court-appointed legal advocate could offer his opinion at a hearing three days later. The judge also ordered both parents not to use corporal punishment on their children.</p><p>The court-appointed advocate’s report or recommendation is not included in available court documents, but a She said the incident as reported by the mother seems more serious than what would be considered acceptable corporal punishment under state law.</p><p>Platt says she understands that people might question why the ex-wife didn’t call the police, but she points out parents might be hesitant to do so for financial and other reasons. She also says it is important not to assume the accusation is untrue because it was made in the context of a contentious divorce and custody battle.</p><p>Yet Platt said it is telling that the sons were allowed to resume overnight, unsupervised visits with Henderson. She is familiar with the person, known as a guardian ad litem, who was appointed to represent Henderson’s sons in court and she says he is well-respected.</p><p>“At times, we always are afraid we're going to miss something, but I don't believe for a second that he would have agreed to this young man returning to his father's care if he thought he was going to get hurt,” she said.</p><p>Court records filed by the guardian ad litem in 2012 said that there had been “serious allegations made by each of the parties which have required investigation by the guardian ad litem.” WBEZ contacted the guardian ad litem and he declined to comment.</p><h3>Do allegations make Henderson unfit to be school board president?</h3><p>Whether Henderson’s actions or views on hitting children as a form of discipline is relevant to being Chicago school board president is up for debate.</p><p>“Parents have different views on corporal punishment, and I respect that,” he said in a written statement. “My own children are now adults, so it is no longer an issue for me.”</p><p>Illinois banned corporal punishment in public schools in 1993. <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/hitting-kids-should-never-be-allowed-illinois-bans-corporal-punishment-in-all-schools" target="_blank" ><u>Two years ago, it became one of the few states</u></a> that also bans the practice in private schools. My personal experiences reinforced for me the importance of carefully evaluating all facts before reaching conclusions.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Everything you need to know about Chicago’s despised parking meters deal
entries.summary: <p>The City Council is facing a Sept. 30 deadline to either approve New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners' $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters, or roll the dice in arbitration and in court.</p><p>Before casting that controversial vote, City Council leaders have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/15/parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-chicago-city-council-brandon-johnson-pat-dowell" >brokered a compromise</a> to try to level the playing field for Chicago taxpayers. What changes did they make? Why is the parking meters deal so controversial? Here's what you need to know: </p><h3>What was so bad about the 2008 parking meters deal?</h3><h3></h3><p>In 2008, then-Mayor Richard M. Daley leased the city’s 36,000 parking meters for 75 years to a private investment consortium for $1.15 billion. He used those proceeds to avoid raising property taxes at a time when city employee pension funds were sinking deeper in the hole. </p><p>The lopsided deal sold off an asset that was generating revenue for the city. Motorists paid the price with steep rate hikes. The Chicago Parking Meters LLC consortium formed by Morgan Stanley, Allianz and Sovereign Wealth recouped their initial $1.15 billion investment by 2019 — roughly 11 years into the 75-year lease.</p><p>Steep rate increases built into the deal would have been bad enough. Rates downtown, for example, rose from $3 an hour in 2008 to $6.50 an hour in 2013. But broken and frozen pay-and-display boxes, along with overstuffed and improperly calibrated meters that overcharged motorists, made it even worse.</p><p>Some motorists were so incensed they vandalized meters and boycotted metered parking, leading to a dramatic drop in on-street parking.</p><p>The deal also required the city to compensate Chicago Parking Meters LLC for every parking space taken out of service, either for a special event or construction project. That part of the deal alone has tied the city’s hands and cost Chicago taxpayers tens of millions of dollars.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-890000" name="image-890000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d9f8b2a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/423a454/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Richard M. Daley at City Hall" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2425424/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Then-Mayor Richard M. Daley, shown at a City Council meeting in 2006.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>M. Spencer Green/Associated Press </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> Daley muscled the deal through the City Council with only five dissenting votes and little debate. But he was forced to acknowledge City Hall botched the transition to private control, and that the turnover should have taken place over a three-to-six month period instead of all at once.</p><p></p><p>No issue in recent memory — not even the Hired Truck and city hiring scandals or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/11/mayor-daley-meigs-field-closure-terrorism-no-fly-zones-northerly-island" >Daley’s notorious midnight destruction of Meigs Field</a> — has resonated more with voters than the parking meter deal.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><h3>What must the Chicago City Council decide now?</h3><p>After making a killing, private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi wanted out and invited bids for Chicago's parking meters.</p><p>Without consulting the Council, Mayor Brandon Johnson submitted a $3.2 billion bid that turned out to be hundreds of millions of dollars higher than the competition.</p><p>But the mayor ultimately abandoned the offer after determining the risk of undoing the parking meter deal was not worth the reward, either financially or politically.</p><p>It would have required the city to pledge to siphon other major sources of revenue the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” or if parking and commuting habits changed.</p><p>That’s a distinct possibility amid a fast-changing landscape for parking demand that includes everything from self-driving vehicles and robot delivery to congestion fees that discourage people from driving downtown.</p><p>After the city dropped out, New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners emerged as the winner with a $2.53 billion bid, pending City Council approval by a revised, Sept. 30 deadline.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" “took the bull by the horns and did the work” to try and, as she put it, “make lemonade out of lemons.” They negotiated an agreement that calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing and 5% of net income going forward — or $376.2 million over the course of the agreement.</p><p>It also would reduce costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p>Stonepeak has also agreed to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. And it has agreed to explore creating entire non-metered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.”</p><p></p><p>The $75 million up-front payment and offer of future profit-sharing may not be enough to garner the 26 votes needed for passage.</p><p>With aldermanic elections less than five months away, some alderpersons may want to push the envelope to see if they get some kind of a break for motorists.</p><p>“City Council members who we’ve been in contact with are still talking. They might be looking at certain points saying, `Hey maybe can we sweeten here, sweeten there?’“ senior mayoral adviser <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/17/chicago-parking-meter-compromise-stonepeak-partners-city-council-mayoral-adviser-jason-lee" >Jason Lee told the Sun-Times. </a>“But in general, the idea that, if you’re going to approve that … you’re going to get concessions that are better for the taxpayers — obviously that is something that we believe is the right direction.”</p><p></p><p></p><h3>What happens if the Council does not approve the compromise deal?</h3><p>The risk to Chicago taxpayers is great. It could cost the city millions.</p><p>The Morgan Stanley-led investment group could first ask an independent arbitrator to order the City Council to approve the sale or pay an exorbitant penalty, then file a lawsuit.</p><p>Former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb, who represents the investment group, wrote a letter to the mayor in June warning the city could face “financial catastrophe” if the sale to Stonepeak Partners is rejected.</p><p>“If the city breaches” the 75-year lease “with the result that the sale to Stonepeak collapses, that will destroy value measures in the billions of dollars for which the city will be held legally responsible,” Webb wrote in the letter.</p><h3>Is that an idle threat? </h3><h3></h3><p>No, it isn’t. Last year, Chicago taxpayers were forced to spend $15.5 million to compensate the investment team that leased the meters, thanks to a risky pandemic-era scheme authorized by former Mayor Lori Lightfoot. As bitter a pill as that was for Chicagoans who despise the deal, it could have been a whole lot worse. The investment group started out by seeking $322 million from the city. An arbitrator recommended $120.7 million. The fact that the Johnson administration managed to persuade Chicago Parking Meters LLC to accept $15.5 million — just 12.8 % of the original demand — was a victory, even though it didn’t seem like it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-140000" name="image-140000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c37352/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/376249e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d96647f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mayor Brandon Johnson announces his bid for re-election Sunday at DuSable Black History Museum Sunday. He gave the Council no direction, possibly concerned there could be political blowback — no matter which way the Council votes.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Man charged after June Kenwood shooting that seriously injured a 15-year-old boy
entries.summary: <p>A 48-year-old Chicago man has been charged with attempted murder after shooting at three people, including a 15-year-old boy who was seriously wounded in June in the Kenwood neighborhood. </p><p>Shauntay Sardin, 48, was charged with three counts of attempted murder because there were two additional victims who were not shot, and aggravated battery, police said.</p><p>On June 20 in the 700 block of East 47th Street, Sardin allegedly opened fire at three people, including a 15-year-old boy who was shot and seriously injured, police said. </p><p>Sardin, of the 1900 block of East 72nd Place in South Shore and who was arrested Monday in the 5100 block of South Indiana Avenue, was due for a detention hearing Tuesday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse <br><b> </b></p>

class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-tu/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>If you name any gospel music star of the mid-20th century, Gregory Donald Gay probably has a story about them. As the younger brother of the Gay Sisters gospel trio, he had a front-row seat for the action during gospel's golden age.</p><p>Now, he is sharing his tales in a recently released book, "Can I Get a Witness! Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music" (The University of Chicago Press). The text was co-written with Steven B. Dolins, the 69-year-old founder and president of The Sirens Records music label in Highland Park.</p><p>Gay's late siblings — Evelyn, Geraldine and Mildred — performed, recorded or rubbed elbows with Clara Ward, Mahalia Jackson, Sam Cooke, the Staple Singers, James Cleveland, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins.</p><p>They released music on the legendary Savoy, Decca and Chess labels, toured the country and helped bring gospel to a televised audience. Their 1951 hit record, "God Will Take Care of You," was later covered by Aretha Franklin.</p><p>But their accomplishments have been overlooked, and their records are difficult to find beyond streaming sites or YouTube.</p><p>Gay said his late sisters would have been forgotten without Dolins.</p><p>"I’m grateful for him opening up a window and letting the general public look in," Gay said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-il/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's your favorite part about fall in Chicago?
